options.a: Demographics, insurance info, chief reason for visit, and provider/time needs
options.b: Demographics and insurance only, leaving the visit reason for the provider to ask
options.c: Insurance info and a copay deposit, with demographics collected at the first visit
options.d: Demographics, insurance info, and a diagnosis code to book the right visit type

distractorExplanations.b: The reason for visit is needed at scheduling to book the right appointment type and slot length; deferring it to the provider causes mis-booked visits.
distractorExplanations.c: Demographics (legal name, DOB, contact) are needed at scheduling for eligibility checks and reminders; a deposit is not a standard scheduling requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: A CMAA does not assign diagnosis codes at scheduling; ICD-10-CM codes come from provider documentation after the encounter, not from the booking call.

options.a: Record each patient's arrival and departure times for the daily flow report
options.b: Block times for visit types, procedures, and provider preferences
options.c: List the day's booked patients with their chart numbers for chart pulling
options.d: Track no-shows and cancellations so they can be charged a missed-visit fee

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a patient-tracking or sign-in log; the matrix is set up in advance to block unavailable times and reserve slots by visit type.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the daily appointment list printed from the schedule, not the matrix, which blocks provider availability before any patient is booked.
distractorExplanations.d: No-show tracking belongs to the no-show policy and log; the scheduling matrix blocks times for visit types, meetings, and provider preferences.

options.a: The schedule is full and a new patient wants the next routine physical
options.b: Two patients each need a long procedure that requires the same exam room
options.c: Two patients can be seen in overlapping slots planned for short visits
options.d: The provider is running late and the remaining slots need to be compressed

distractorExplanations.a: New-patient physicals need full-length slots; double-booking long visits creates backlog, so the patient should be offered the next real opening.
distractorExplanations.b: Overlapping long procedures that need one room guarantees delays; double-booking suits brief visits that can share a provider's time.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressing slots when the provider is behind worsens delays; the CMAA should update waiting patients and offer to reschedule instead.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-scheduling-fron.explanation: Intentional overlap differs from chaotic overbooking; communicate wait times. Overlap works only when it fits the provider's workflow.

options.a: Move the late patient ahead of on-time patients so the delay stays short for them
options.b: Reschedule every late arrival on the spot, whether 2 or 20 minutes late
options.c: Check them in without comment and let them wait for the next open gap in the day
options.d: Follow office policy—possibly reschedule or fit in without disrupting critical care

distractorExplanations.a: Bumping on-time patients rewards lateness and spreads the delay to others; office policy decides whether to fit in or reschedule a late arrival.
distractorExplanations.b: Blanket rescheduling ignores the grace window most late-arrival policies set; many offices fit in patients who are only a few minutes late.
distractorExplanations.c: Silent waiting is poor service; the CMAA should explain the expected wait or options under policy so the patient can decide to stay or rebook.

options.a: Insurance authorization/referral numbers and specialist network status
options.b: The patient's copay amount and the specialist's office hours and location
options.c: The referring provider's NPI and the patient's preferred appointment days
options.d: The specialist's fee schedule and the amount of deductible met to date

distractorExplanations.b: Copay and logistics are useful but do not prevent denials; a referral visit needs the authorization/referral number and in-network status confirmed.
distractorExplanations.c: The NPI goes on the claim and preferences help booking, but neither confirms the authorization or network status the payer requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost estimates help with financial counseling, but without a valid referral/authorization and a network check the specialist claim can still be denied.

options.a: Patients booked at fixed, evenly spaced intervals, one per time slot
options.b: Several patients scheduled at the same hour and seen in arrival/order workflow
options.c: Similar visit types grouped together in one block, such as all physicals
options.d: Patients seen in order of arrival during set open hours without booked times

distractorExplanations.a: That is stream (time-specified) scheduling, where each patient gets an individual slot; wave books several patients at the top of the hour.
distractorExplanations.c: Grouping similar visits (all physicals in one block) is cluster or categorization scheduling, not wave scheduling.
distractorExplanations.d: Seeing patients as they arrive with no appointments is open-hours (walk-in) scheduling; wave scheduling still books patients to a set hour.

options.a: Serve as the legal record of the visit in place of the progress note
options.b: Request prior authorization from the payer before the visit takes place
options.c: Capture services/procedures/diagnoses for billing from the visit
options.d: Show the patient's itemized balance due after insurance has paid

distractorExplanations.a: The superbill is a billing document; the provider's documentation in the chart remains the legal record that must support every code billed.
distractorExplanations.b: Prior authorization is a separate pre-visit request to the payer; the encounter form captures what was done and diagnosed at the visit.
distractorExplanations.d: An itemized balance after insurance payment is the patient statement, which is produced later from posted payments, not the encounter form.

options.a: Applied consistently, documented, and explained in patient communications
options.b: Applied at staff discretion, waiving fees for patients the staff know well
options.c: Explained to patients only after their first missed appointment occurs
options.d: Documented in the staff manual but kept off patient forms to avoid conflict

distractorExplanations.b: Discretionary enforcement is inconsistent and can look discriminatory; a no-show policy must be applied the same way to every patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Patients must learn the policy before it applies, at registration or scheduling; explaining it only after a miss makes enforcement unfair.
distractorExplanations.d: A policy patients never see cannot fairly be enforced; it must be explained in patient communications as well as documented internally.

options.a: Several patients at the top of each hour, seen as they arrive
options.b: Similar appointments together (e.g., all physicals in a block)
options.c: Open walk-in hours together at the start and end of each clinic day
options.d: Patients by insurance plan so their claims can be batched by payer

distractorExplanations.a: Booking several patients at the top of the hour and seeing them as they arrive is wave scheduling, not clustering by visit type.
distractorExplanations.c: Reserving walk-in periods is open-hours scheduling; cluster scheduling groups like appointments (for example physicals) into a block.
distractorExplanations.d: Batching claims by payer is a billing workflow; cluster scheduling groups similar visit types to use rooms, equipment, and staff efficiently.

options.a: Give each patient a fixed, evenly spaced slot so waiting stays minimal
options.b: Schedule multiple patients at the same arrival time to improve flow
options.c: Group similar visit types into blocks so rooms and equipment are ready
options.d: Let patients arrive any time during set hours without booked appointments

distractorExplanations.a: Evenly spaced individual slots describe stream (time-specified) scheduling; wave scheduling deliberately books several patients at one time.
distractorExplanations.c: Grouping like visits into blocks is cluster scheduling, which organizes by appointment type rather than by shared arrival times.
distractorExplanations.d: Arrival without booked times is open-hours (walk-in) scheduling; wave scheduling still assigns patients to a specific hour.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-scheduling-fron.explanation: Wave scheduling clusters arrivals to reduce idle provider time while managing wait. Patients are then seen in arrival order within the hour.

options.a: The patient's card copy and photo ID, which together confirm active coverage
options.b: Eligibility, coverage, and referral/authorization requirements
options.c: Eligibility only, since authorization is the specialist's responsibility
options.d: The copay amount and the provider's fee schedule for planned services

distractorExplanations.a: A card copy and ID confirm identity, not current eligibility; coverage can lapse, so the plan must be verified with the payer before the visit.
distractorExplanations.c: The ordering or referring office often must obtain the referral or authorization; skipping that check leads to denials and surprise bills.
distractorExplanations.d: Copay is one benefit detail, but it does not confirm eligibility, covered services, or whether a referral or authorization is required.

options.a: Enforced case by case depending on each patient's history
options.b: Clearly communicated, consistently applied, and documented
options.c: Posted at the front desk but applied only to new patients
options.d: Strict enough to discharge a patient after the first missed visit

distractorExplanations.a: Case-by-case enforcement is inconsistent and invites discrimination complaints; an effective no-show policy is applied the same way to everyone.
distractorExplanations.c: Applying the policy to new patients and not established ones is inconsistent; the policy must cover all patients and be documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Discharge after a single no-show is excessive; most policies use progressive steps such as reminders, warnings, and written notice first.

options.a: Accurate legal name, DOB, contact, and insurance identifiers
options.b: Preferred name, DOB, and emergency contact, with insurance added at billing
options.c: Legal name, Social Security number, and employer as the main identifiers
options.d: Legal name, chief complaint, and allergies entered by the front desk

distractorExplanations.b: A preferred name does not replace the legal name, and insurance identifiers are needed at registration so eligibility can be verified before the visit.
distractorExplanations.c: The SSN is not required for registration and should be minimized; DOB, contact details, and insurance identifiers are the essentials.
distractorExplanations.d: Chief complaint and allergies are clinical intake documented by clinical staff, not core demographic registration data for the CMAA.

options.a: Seat whichever patient checked in first and ask the other to rebook
options.b: Review the schedule/documentation calmly and escalate per office protocol
options.c: Have both patients wait while the provider decides who will be seen first
options.d: Apologize and see both by shortening each visit to fit into the one slot

distractorExplanations.a: First to check in ignores the actual booking record; the CMAA should verify the schedule before deciding who keeps the slot.
distractorExplanations.c: Schedule conflicts are an administrative task; the CMAA verifies the record and escalates to the office manager, not the treating provider.
distractorExplanations.d: Halving two visits to fit one slot compromises care for both patients; the conflict should be resolved by reviewing the schedule.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-scheduling-fron.explanation: De-escalate, verify records, and follow protocol; protect privacy while resolving errors. The goal is to resolve the conflict without blaming either patient.

options.a: Documentation of care used for clinical, legal, and billing purposes
options.b: All EHR data, including audit logs, drafts, and staff messages
options.c: The provider's personal notes kept separately from the patient's chart
options.d: The billing record of charges and payments for each patient encounter

distractorExplanations.b: The legal health record is the set the organization designates as the official chart; audit metadata, drafts, and internal messages are usually excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Personal working notes kept outside the chart are not part of the designated legal record; the legal record is the official documentation of care.
distractorExplanations.d: The financial record supports billing but is not the clinical documentation of care that serves clinical, legal, and billing purposes.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-medical-records.explanation: Entries should be timely, accurate, authenticated, and complete. It must be kept under state and facility retention rules.

options.a: Marketing communications sent by the practice about third-party products
options.b: Treatment, payment, and healthcare operations (TPO) under the Privacy Rule
options.c: Psychotherapy notes requested by the patient's health plan for payment
options.d: Employer requests for a worker's health status for a hiring decision

distractorExplanations.a: Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, using PHI for marketing third-party products generally requires the patient's written authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Psychotherapy notes have special protection and need a specific authorization even when a health plan requests them for payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers need the employee's authorization (or another legal basis such as workers' comp) to receive PHI; employment decisions are not TPO.

options.a: Patient signature and date, with recipient and purpose added later by staff
options.b: The requesting provider's signature with the patient's verbal consent noted
options.c: Who, what, to whom, purpose, expiration, and signature/date elements
options.d: Patient name, record type, and signature, with no expiration required

distractorExplanations.a: Staff cannot complete core elements after the patient signs; recipient, purpose, and expiration must be on the form when it is signed.
distractorExplanations.b: A HIPAA authorization must be signed by the patient or personal representative; a provider signature plus verbal consent is not valid.
distractorExplanations.d: An expiration date or expiration event is a required core element; an authorization without one is defective and should be returned.

options.a: Overwriting the error once the provider approves so the record stays clean
options.b: Deleting the incorrect entry and re-entering it with the original date
options.c: Fixing another clinician's note directly when the error is clerical
options.d: Addendum/correction that preserves the original entry (no obliteration)

distractorExplanations.a: Overwriting erases the original entry; even with approval, corrections must be addenda that keep the original visible in the audit trail.
distractorExplanations.b: Deleting and backdating hides the error; a correction must be dated and timed when made, with the original entry preserved.
distractorExplanations.c: Only the author (or per policy, a designee) corrects an entry; other staff notify the author instead of editing someone else's note.

options.a: Follow federal/state timelines and facility procedures with tracking logs
options.b: Allow up to 90 days for any request, since HIPAA sets no deadline at all
options.c: Be completed the same day for every request, before identity is verified
options.d: Be set by the requester, who may demand release within 24 hours

distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA requires action on access requests within 30 days, with one 30-day extension; states may set shorter limits, never a 90-day default.
distractorExplanations.c: Identity and authority must be verified before any release; HIPAA does not require same-day turnaround, it sets a 30-day limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Requesters cannot set legal timelines; federal (30-day HIPAA) and state rules plus facility procedure govern turnaround.

options.a: Business associates so they know how to use and protect the practice's PHI
options.b: Patients to explain uses of PHI and patient rights, with acknowledgment efforts
options.c: Patients only when they request a copy of their medical records
options.d: Health plans and payers before the practice submits the first claim

distractorExplanations.a: Business associates are bound by a business associate agreement; the NPP is a patient-facing notice of uses, disclosures, and rights.
distractorExplanations.c: The NPP is provided at the first service delivery with a good-faith effort to get acknowledgment, not only when records are requested.
distractorExplanations.d: Payers do not receive the NPP; it is given to patients to explain how PHI is used and what rights they have.

options.a: Disclose only the diagnosis code, even when a provider requests it for treatment
options.b: Collect the fewest demographics possible at registration to limit risk
options.c: Limit PHI access/use/disclosure to the least needed for the purpose
options.d: Give staff access to any chart once they sign a confidentiality form

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosures to another provider for treatment are exempt from minimum necessary; withholding needed clinical detail can harm care.
distractorExplanations.b: Minimum necessary limits use and disclosure of PHI, not the collection of required registration data such as legal name, DOB, and insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Signing a confidentiality form does not grant access; role-based limits still restrict each workforce member to the PHI their job requires.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-medical-records.explanation: Role-based access implements minimum necessary. Disclosures to providers for treatment are exempt from the standard.

options.a: Set by HIPAA at a uniform 6 years from the last visit for all records
options.b: Fixed at 7 years nationally by CMS for every patient's chart
options.c: Tied to the age of majority plus a set number of years
options.d: Governed by state law and payer/accreditation policies

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA's 6-year rule covers HIPAA documentation such as policies and authorizations, not medical record retention, which state law governs.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no single national 7-year rule; CMS and other payer periods vary by program, and state law sets the baseline for records.
distractorExplanations.c: Age-of-majority rules extend retention for minors' records; adult record retention is set by state law and payer/accreditation policy.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-medical-records.explanation: Know that retention varies; follow the strictest applicable rule/policy. Periods often run years beyond the last visit.

options.a: Someone with legal authority (eg, healthcare power of attorney)
options.b: The adult patient's spouse, who may sign authorizations by default
options.c: Any adult child listed as the emergency contact on registration
options.d: A family member who brings the patient to visits and pays the bill

distractorExplanations.b: Marriage alone does not make someone a HIPAA personal representative; legal authority such as a healthcare POA or guardianship is required.
distractorExplanations.c: Being the emergency contact does not create legal authority to act for the patient or sign authorizations for release of PHI.
distractorExplanations.d: Involvement in care or paying the bill may allow limited sharing, but it does not confer personal-representative authority.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-medical-records.explanation: Verify authority before discussing PHI or obtaining authorizations. Who qualifies is defined by state law.

options.a: Using a cover sheet and sending the full chart so the recipient has context
options.b: Verifying numbers, using cover sheets, and placing machines in secure areas
options.c: Faxing to the recipient's main number and calling afterward to confirm
options.d: Including the diagnosis on the cover sheet so staff route it correctly

distractorExplanations.a: A cover sheet helps, but faxing the full chart violates minimum necessary, and the number still must be verified before sending.
distractorExplanations.c: Confirming after transmission does not prevent misdirection; the number should be verified or preprogrammed before PHI is sent.
distractorExplanations.d: The cover sheet should carry a confidentiality notice and contacts, not PHI such as a diagnosis that anyone near the machine can read.

options.a: Electronic health records only, not paper charts or spoken information
options.b: Individually identifiable health information in any form
options.c: Health information de-identified under the Safe Harbor method
options.d: Employment records held by a covered entity in its role as employer

distractorExplanations.a: Electronic-only describes ePHI under the Security Rule; the Privacy Rule protects identifiable health information on paper, orally, and electronically.
distractorExplanations.c: Information properly de-identified under Safe Harbor (18 identifiers removed) is no longer PHI and is outside the Privacy Rule.
distractorExplanations.d: HIPAA expressly excludes employment records a covered entity holds as an employer from the definition of PHI.

options.a: A written request from the third party on its letterhead with a purpose
options.b: A valid patient authorization (or another permitted disclosure)
options.c: The patient's verbal permission by phone, noted in the chart by the CMAA
options.d: A signed general consent to treat from the first visit

distractorExplanations.a: A requester's letter is not the patient's authorization; non-TPO releases need the patient's signed authorization or another HIPAA pathway.
distractorExplanations.c: A HIPAA authorization must be written and signed with required core elements; a charted verbal permission does not meet that standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Consent to treatment is not a HIPAA authorization; releasing records to a third party needs a specific authorization covering the request.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-medical-records.explanation: Most non-TPO disclosures require proper authorization or another HIPAA pathway. The authorization must cover the specific request.

options.a: The HIPAA six-year rule applied to every medical record
options.b: State law, payer, and facility retention policies
options.c: Accreditation guidance, which overrides state statutes
options.d: The provider's preference, as long as records are kept secure

distractorExplanations.a: HIPAA's 6-year retention applies to HIPAA compliance documentation, not to medical records, which follow state law and payer rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Accreditation bodies can add requirements but do not override state law; retention follows state law, payer, and facility policy together.
distractorExplanations.d: Retention periods are set by law and organizational policy, not by individual provider preference, even when storage is secure.

options.a: Every staff member can view any chart after signing a confidentiality pledge
options.b: Workforce members access only the PHI needed for their job functions
options.c: Patients can view their own records through the patient portal on request
options.d: Clinicians can edit any entry, while front desk staff may view all charts

distractorExplanations.a: A signed pledge does not grant access; role-based controls limit each user to the PHI their job requires under minimum necessary.
distractorExplanations.c: Portal access implements the patient's right of access; role-based access controls govern what workforce members can see.
distractorExplanations.d: Front desk staff need scheduling and demographic data, not every chart; role-based access restricts both viewing and editing by role.

options.a: Procedures and services performed
options.b: Diagnoses and reasons for the visit
options.c: Supplies, drugs, and ambulance services
options.d: Inpatient hospital procedures

distractorExplanations.b: Diagnoses and reasons for the visit are reported with ICD-10-CM codes; CPT describes the procedures and services performed.
distractorExplanations.c: Supplies, drugs, and ambulance services are reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not with CPT (HCPCS Level I) codes.
distractorExplanations.d: Inpatient facility procedures are coded with ICD-10-PCS; CPT is used for physician and outpatient procedures and services.

options.a: The service was not authorized by the payer before the visit date
options.b: The claim was submitted after the payer's deadline
options.c: The payer did not process the claim within its required timeframe
options.d: The claim was filed before the patient's eligibility was verified

distractorExplanations.a: A missing authorization produces a prior-authorization denial; timely filing means the claim reached the payer after its deadline.
distractorExplanations.c: Payer delays fall under prompt-pay rules; a timely filing denial is about the provider submitting the claim too late.
distractorExplanations.d: Unverified coverage leads to an eligibility denial if the patient was not covered; timely filing concerns the submission deadline.

options.a: How much the patient owes after the deductible has been met
options.b: Whether a service requires preauthorization before it is performed
options.c: Which insurance pays first when a patient has multiple coverages
options.d: Which provider is paid when two physicians bill the same service

distractorExplanations.a: What the patient owes after the deductible is coinsurance or copay cost-sharing under one plan, not coordination of benefits.
distractorExplanations.b: Preauthorization rules are set by each plan's utilization management; COB decides which of several plans pays first.
distractorExplanations.d: Two providers billing one service triggers duplicate-claim edits; COB applies when one patient has more than one insurance plan.

options.a: Medicaid services that need prior authorization from the state
options.b: Commercial plans' explanation of benefits sent after a claim is paid
options.c: Medicare patients' notice explaining how a processed claim was paid
options.d: Medicare situations where a service may not be covered

distractorExplanations.a: The ABN is an Original Medicare form; Medicaid prior authorization is a separate state process, not an advance beneficiary notice.
distractorExplanations.b: An EOB is sent by commercial payers after processing; the ABN is given to Medicare patients before a possibly noncovered service.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the Medicare Summary Notice (MSN), sent after processing; the ABN is issued before the service is provided.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-billing-coding-.explanation: Proper ABN issuance matters before the service when required. The ABN warns the patient before the service that they may be financially liable.

options.a: Provider documentation to the highest specificity supported
options.b: The diagnosis on the referral or order, even if the note differs
options.c: The superbill's preprinted code closest to the patient's complaint
options.d: Probable or rule-out diagnoses from the outpatient visit

distractorExplanations.b: Codes come from the encounter's provider documentation; when the order and the note differ, the documented diagnosis governs.
distractorExplanations.c: The nearest preprinted code often lacks specificity; the code must match what the provider documented to the highest supported detail.
distractorExplanations.d: Outpatient guidelines prohibit coding uncertain diagnoses (probable, rule out); code the documented signs and symptoms instead.

options.a: Has been paid in full by the primary payer with no patient balance
options.b: Has complete/accurate data enabling payer processing
options.c: Was submitted electronically rather than on a paper CMS-1500
options.d: Passed the clearinghouse scrubber, even if the payer later pends it

distractorExplanations.a: Clean describes an accurate, complete submission, not the payment outcome; a clean claim can still leave a patient balance.
distractorExplanations.c: Submission format does not define a clean claim; a paper CMS-1500 can be clean, and an electronic claim can be missing data.
distractorExplanations.d: Passing scrubber edits is not enough; a claim the payer pends for missing information is by definition not clean.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-billing-coding-.explanation: Front-desk data quality (subscriber ID, DOB, NPI, POS) drives clean claims. A clean claim does not pend for missing information.

options.a: Daily appointments, no-shows, and cancellations by provider
options.b: Payroll hours, overtime, and employee reimbursements
options.c: Charges, payments, adjustments, and outstanding balances
options.d: Supply orders, invoices due, and vendor payments

distractorExplanations.a: Appointments, no-shows, and cancellations are tracked on the schedule and appointment log, not on the day sheet or A/R ledger.
distractorExplanations.b: Payroll and employee reimbursements are expenses handled by payroll and accounts payable, not patient accounts receivable.
distractorExplanations.d: Vendor invoices and payments are accounts payable (money the office owes); A/R tracks money owed to the office by patients and payers.

options.a: A bilateral procedure is performed during the same operative session
options.b: A distinct procedural service is performed at a separate site that day
options.c: A clinical diagnostic lab test is repeated on the same day for new results
options.d: A significant, separately identifiable E/M is billed same day as a procedure

distractorExplanations.a: Bilateral procedures in one session use modifier 50, not modifier 25, which is for a separate E/M on the day of a procedure.
distractorExplanations.b: A distinct procedure at a separate site is reported with modifier 59 (or X{EPSU}); modifier 25 attaches to the E/M code.
distractorExplanations.c: A repeated clinical diagnostic lab test on the same day uses modifier 91; modifier 25 is for a separately identifiable E/M.

options.a: Clearly show dates of service, charges, payments, and amount due
options.b: Show the balance due only, so patients aren't confused by line items
options.c: Show charges and balance due, with insurance payments left to the EOB
options.d: Be mailed in envelopes showing the specialty, such as 'Oncology Billing'

distractorExplanations.b: Patients need itemized dates, charges, and payments to understand and verify a bill; a bare balance invites disputes.
distractorExplanations.c: Insurance payments and adjustments belong on the statement so the patient sees how the balance was reached, not only on the EOB.
distractorExplanations.d: A specialty name on the envelope discloses PHI to anyone handling the mail; statements should use a neutral return address.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-billing-coding-.explanation: Transparent billing is ethical and often regulated by state rules. They should also list a contact for billing questions.

options.a: A guarantee that the payer will pay once the service is approved
options.b: Payer approval processes required before certain services for coverage
options.c: The patient's signed consent agreeing to the procedure and its risks
options.d: Payer review of medical necessity after the claim has been submitted

distractorExplanations.a: Authorization is not a payment guarantee; claims can still be denied for eligibility lapses, benefit limits, or medical necessity.
distractorExplanations.c: Informed consent is a clinical agreement between patient and provider; preauthorization is an approval obtained from the payer.
distractorExplanations.d: Review after submission is retrospective or post-payment review; preauthorization and precertification happen before the service.

options.a: The fixed dollar amount the patient pays at each office visit for covered care
options.b: The amount the patient must pay before the plan begins paying covered services
options.c: The percentage of covered costs the patient pays after meeting the deductible
options.d: The monthly amount the patient pays to keep the insurance plan in force

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed amount paid at each visit is a copayment; the deductible is the total the patient pays before the plan starts paying.
distractorExplanations.c: A percentage paid after the deductible is coinsurance; the deductible itself is the amount paid before plan payments begin.
distractorExplanations.d: The monthly payment to keep coverage active is the premium, which is separate from the deductible and other cost-sharing.

options.a: A patient's plan requires a primary care referral before a specialist visit
options.b: A patient has more than one insurance plan that may cover the same services
options.c: A patient's claim is split between the deductible and coinsurance
options.d: A patient changes plans mid-year and the old plan has already ended

distractorExplanations.a: Referral requirements are a gatekeeper rule of one plan (often an HMO); COB applies when two or more plans cover the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Splitting a claim between deductible and coinsurance is cost-sharing within one plan, not coordination between multiple plans.
distractorExplanations.d: With no overlap in coverage there is nothing to coordinate; services after the change are simply billed to the new plan.

options.a: Payments received and adjustments posted to accounts that day
options.b: Common diagnoses and procedures to support charge capture for a visit
options.c: The patient's itemized charges and balance due after insurance
options.d: Payer-approved services and authorization numbers for the visit

distractorExplanations.a: Daily payments and adjustments are recorded on the day sheet; the superbill captures the visit's diagnoses and procedures.
distractorExplanations.c: Itemized charges and balance after insurance appear on the patient statement, produced after claims are processed.
distractorExplanations.d: Authorization numbers are tracked in the authorization log or referral record, not preprinted on the encounter form.

options.a: File a formal appeal with the payer before reviewing the denial reason code
options.b: Review the denial reason, correct the claim/documentation, and resubmit or appeal
options.c: Bill the patient for the full amount until the payer reprocesses the claim
options.d: Resubmit the same claim right away, since most missing-info denials clear

distractorExplanations.a: Missing-information denials are fixed by correcting and resubmitting; appealing without reading the reason code wastes time.
distractorExplanations.c: Shifting a payer-side billing error to the patient is improper; the office must correct the claim before billing any patient balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Resubmitting an unchanged claim triggers a duplicate or repeat denial; the missing information must be added first.

options.a: Paraphrasing, clarifying, and attending to verbal/nonverbal cues
options.b: Preparing your reply while the patient finishes explaining the concern
options.c: Typing the patient's words verbatim while keeping eyes on the screen
options.d: Offering quick reassurance so the patient feels heard right away

distractorExplanations.b: Planning a reply while the patient talks splits attention and misses details; active listening means attending, then paraphrasing.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbatim typing with eyes on the screen ignores nonverbal cues such as tone and body language, which active listening requires.
distractorExplanations.d: Premature reassurance is a recognized communication barrier; it cuts off the patient before the concern is understood and clarified.

options.a: Ask the patient to leave and reschedule before hearing the complaint
options.b: Stay calm, set boundaries, ensure safety, and involve supervisor/security
options.c: Explain the policy firmly and repeat it until the patient accepts it
options.d: Handle it alone at the desk so other staff aren't pulled from their work

distractorExplanations.a: Dismissing an upset patient without listening usually escalates the situation; de-escalation starts with calm acknowledgment.
distractorExplanations.c: Repeating policy at an angry patient escalates conflict; acknowledge feelings, set boundaries, and bring in a supervisor if needed.
distractorExplanations.d: Hostile encounters need supervisor or security involvement for safety; handling them alone puts the CMAA and other patients at risk.

options.a: Means feeling sorry for the patient and expressing pity for their difficult situation
options.b: Involves sharing the same emotion as the patient to show that you truly care
options.c: Seeks to understand the patient's feelings without necessarily sharing the same emotion
options.d: Focuses on fixing the patient's problem quickly rather than on how they feel

distractorExplanations.a: Feeling sorry for and pitying the patient describes sympathy; empathy is understanding the patient's perspective without pity.
distractorExplanations.b: Taking on the patient's emotion is sympathy or emotional contagion; empathy understands feelings while staying professionally steady.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping to fix the problem is problem-solving, not empathy; empathy first acknowledges and understands the patient's feelings.

options.a: Sharing patient details with coworkers as long as they work in the clinic
options.b: Discussing cases freely once the patient's name has been left out
options.c: Releasing information to family members who call asking about the patient
options.d: Not discussing patient information with unauthorized persons

distractorExplanations.a: Working in the same clinic does not give a need to know; patient information is shared only with staff who need it for their role.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the name alone does not de-identify a case; age, condition, and visit details can still identify the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Family callers need the patient's agreement or personal-representative authority before PHI is shared with them.

options.a: Friending patients on social media to keep them engaged
options.b: Avoiding dual relationships that exploit patients
options.c: Offering favored patients priority slots in return for small gifts
options.d: Sharing personal problems with patients to build rapport and trust

distractorExplanations.a: Personal social media connections with patients blur professional boundaries and create privacy risks; use official practice channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Trading scheduling priority for gifts creates favoritism and a conflict of interest; gift policies exist to prevent exactly this.
distractorExplanations.d: Personal self-disclosure reverses the professional relationship and shifts focus to the staff member; rapport comes from respectful service.

nha-cmaa-readiness-check-communication-e.explanation: Follow office policies on gifts/relationships. Communications with patients should stay professional and appropriate.

options.a: Wait until it happens again before raising it with anyone
options.b: Report it straight to the patient so they can file a complaint
options.c: Remind them of privacy rules and report per policy if needed
options.d: Leave it to the privacy officer to catch in the next audit

distractorExplanations.a: A single overheard disclosure is already a privacy breach; it should be addressed promptly rather than waiting for a pattern.
distractorExplanations.b: Breach assessment and patient notification are handled by the privacy officer under policy, not by an individual coworker.
distractorExplanations.d: Audits of EHR access do not capture verbal gossip; workforce members are expected to speak up and report per policy.

options.a: The CMAA who schedules the procedure and collects the signed form
options.b: The nurse or MA who prepares the patient on the day of the procedure
options.c: The facility's risk manager, who reviews consent forms for legal accuracy
options.d: The provider performing the procedure, with CMAA supporting forms/logistics

distractorExplanations.a: A CMAA may provide forms or witness a signature but cannot explain risks, benefits, and alternatives, which is the provider's duty.
distractorExplanations.b: Clinical staff may reinforce teaching, but the legal duty to disclose risks and obtain informed consent rests with the performing provider.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk management designs and audits consent forms; it does not conduct the informed consent discussion with the patient.

options.a: Apology, correction, and prevention steps without blaming the patient
options.b: A discount on the visit in place of correcting the registration record
options.c: Correcting the record quietly without telling the patient about the error
options.d: An apology and an explanation of which staff member made the mistake

distractorExplanations.b: Compensation does not fix the error; the registration record must be corrected or the mistake will cause claim and safety problems.
distractorExplanations.c: Quiet correction skips the apology and transparency that rebuild trust; service recovery includes acknowledging the error.
distractorExplanations.d: Naming a coworker shifts blame and looks unprofessional; service recovery focuses on fixing the error and preventing a repeat.

options.a: Settled informally between the coworkers involved before any report to HR
options.b: Reported per HR policy; patients and staff deserve a respectful environment
options.c: Reported only when a witness can confirm what happened
options.d: Tolerated when the harasser is a patient, since patients aren't employees

distractorExplanations.a: Requiring informal resolution first deters reporting and can expose victims; harassment should be reported through HR policy.
distractorExplanations.c: A witness is not required to report harassment; employers must investigate complaints and protect reporters from retaliation.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers must also protect staff from harassment by patients and other third parties; it is reported and addressed under policy.

options.a: Leave the test name and result, since it is the patient's own voicemail
options.b: Leave minimal necessary information per policy to protect privacy
options.c: Give the results to the spouse who answers, since family can relay them
options.d: Ask whoever answers to confirm the patient's DOB, then share results

distractorExplanations.a: Others may hear a home or shared voicemail; messages should give only minimum necessary details such as name and callback number.
distractorExplanations.c: A spouse is not authorized by default; results go to the patient unless the patient has agreed to share them with that person.
distractorExplanations.d: A third party who knows the DOB is still not the patient; confirming a DOB does not authorize disclosure to that person.

options.a: Agreeing with the patient's complaint to calm them, even if it's inaccurate
options.b: Acknowledging feelings while remaining professional and solution-focused
options.c: Sharing a similar personal experience so the patient feels less alone
options.d: Waiving policies like late fees whenever the patient seems upset

distractorExplanations.a: Agreeing with inaccurate claims misleads the patient; empathy acknowledges feelings without endorsing incorrect facts.
distractorExplanations.c: Personal self-disclosure shifts the focus to the staff member; empathy keeps attention on the patient's feelings and needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Empathy does not mean abandoning policy; it acknowledges feelings while applying office policies consistently.

options.a: Referring patients to the provider's chosen in-network lab
options.b: Accepting kickbacks to refer patients to a specific vendor
options.c: Declining a patient's small holiday gift per office gift policy
options.d: Scheduling a relative as a patient using the standard booking rules

distractorExplanations.a: Using a provider-selected in-network lab is a normal referral practice with no personal gain to the CMAA, so it is not a conflict.
distractorExplanations.c: Following the gift policy is how staff avoid conflicts of interest; declining a gift is not itself a conflict.
distractorExplanations.d: A conflict arises when personal interest changes decisions; booking a relative under the same rules as everyone else does not.

options.a: Ask the patient's adult family member to interpret the consent forms
options.b: Use a qualified interpreter/service per facility policy
options.c: Use a bilingual coworker from billing who speaks the patient's language
options.d: Give the patient English forms and a translation app to complete alone

distractorExplanations.a: Family interpreters may omit or alter content and compromise privacy; Section 1557 favors qualified interpreters for medical communication.
distractorExplanations.c: Speaking a language is not the same as being a qualified medical interpreter; untrained staff can mistranslate clinical terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Machine translation is unreliable for medical and consent content; patients with limited English need a qualified interpreter.

options.a: Giving patients your personal cell number for faster scheduling
options.b: Maintaining a therapeutic, respectful relationship without exploitation
options.c: Accepting a patient's offer of free services from their own business
options.d: Looking up a friend's chart to update them on their test results

distractorExplanations.a: Personal phone contact blurs professional boundaries and bypasses documented office channels; scheduling goes through the practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Free services from a patient create a dual relationship and a sense of obligation, which crosses professional boundaries.
distractorExplanations.d: Accessing a chart without a job need violates HIPAA, and giving results is outside the CMAA role even for a friend.
